newsitem.title: CROATIA: Thousands of Croats protest radio shutdown.
newsitem.headline: Thousands of Croats protest radio shutdown.

text.p: Thousands of people demonstrated in the Croatian capital on Wednesday to protest the government's bid to shut down an influential independent radio station.
The largest public protest in years came after the rightist government awarded the radio's frequency to a rival station which does yet exist.
"It is a tragedy that after 12 years of fighting for democracy and civil society the radio is to be shut down like this," said editor Zrinka Vrabec-Mojzes.
"But we are going to use all legal means to fight against this absurd decision," she told Reuters.
News that the radio could not broadcast after November 30 brought an avalanche of protests from listeners.
Opposition party leaders, soldiers, students, journalists from other Croatian media, trade unions and ordinary citizens were calling in to express their support.
An army captain publically renounced his rank and half a dozen medals he was awarded by President Franjo Tudjman for fighting for Croatia's independence.
A university professor said it was "a dark day for Croatia and its democracy".
A leading state television anchorman said the decision was "catastrophic".
A war invalid had a message to the authorities which summarised the public reaction: "You can take everything from us, but you can't take Radio 101."
Several thousand people answered a call of Zagreb soccer fan club Croatia to gather at a downtown square for a token protest.
The crowd shouted abuses against Tudjman and his ruling party, and waved banners in support of the radio. One read: "The eleventh commandment: 'Don't turn off Radio 101'".
The radio kept airing telegrams of support from all over the country well into the evening.
"The support of the citizens shows that democracy cannot be supressed," said Zdravko Tomac, a leader of the reformed communist party.
The United States ambassador to Croatia, Peter Galbraith also appeared on the show, saying Washington was closely following the issue.
"I have come here because your case raises important questions whether there can be free broadcast media in Croatia," Galbraith said.
As he spoke dozens of taxi drivers sounded their horns in support.
The owner of the rival Globus Radio 101, a non-existent radio which was awarded the frequency, said he would renounce the concession.
Media tycoon Nino Pavic, closely linked to the ruling HDZ party, said: "If our getting the concession is seen as threatening media freedom, we don't want to be a part of it."
Even some HDZ leaders, clearly taken aback by the protests, started to back away from the decision.
The head of the HDZ city comittee Zlatko Canjuga told the radio: "If the decision was made, it does not mean that it cannot be reversed".
Radio 101 was founded 12 years ago and tried to promote free speech when Croatia was part of former communist Yugoslavia.
It was the first media outlet to let Tudjman to speak in public in 1990 when he was branded by the communist state media as a "person with dangerous intent".
